key_terms.meaning: H = U + PV, the heat exchanged at constant pressure; ΔH is negative for an exothermic reaction
A measure of energy dispersal; ΔS = q_rev/T for a reversible change, in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹
G = H − TS; at constant temperature and pressure a process is spontaneous only if ΔG < 0
A change that proceeds on its own without continuous outside work; ΔG < 0 at constant T and P
An equation linking rate to concentrations, such as rate = k[A]ᵐ[B]ⁿ
The sum of the concentration powers in the experimental rate law; m + n above
The proportionality constant in a rate law, fixed at a given temperature, units depend on order
The number of species colliding in a single elementary step; a whole number, 1, 2 or rarely 3
k = A e^(−Ea/RT), with A the pre-exponential factor and Ea the activation energy in J mol⁻¹
The slowest elementary step of a mechanism; it fixes the overall rate law
The product formed fastest wins, because the reaction is irreversible or short; the less stable product may dominate
The most stable product (lowest G) wins, reached when the reaction is reversible and given enough time or heat
A physically distinct and mechanically separable part of a system; ice, water and vapour are three phases
The smallest number of independent chemical species needed to write the composition of every phase
The number of intensive variables (T, P, composition) that can be varied independently without changing the number of phases
F = C − P + 2, where C is components, P is phases and 2 counts temperature and pressure
The single temperature and pressure where three phases coexist; for water 273.16 K and 611.7 Pa
The temperature and pressure above which liquid and vapour cannot be told apart; for water 647 K and 22.06 MPa
The composition and temperature where a liquid freezes as two solids together; the lowest melting point of the pair
F′ = C − P + 1, used for condensed systems where pressure is fixed at 1 atm

takeaways: Energy alone does not decide whether a change happens; enthalpy and entropy act together, and Gibbs free energy combines them into one test.
ΔG = ΔH − TΔS shows why heating can turn a non-spontaneous reaction spontaneous: the −TΔS term grows.
A rate law comes from experiment, not from the balanced equation; order and molecularity are therefore different ideas.
The rate constant rises exponentially with temperature, so a 10 K rise roughly doubles many reaction rates near room temperature.
A mechanism is a sequence of elementary steps; the slowest step writes the rate law and the other steps stay hidden.
Fastest product and stablest product differ; low temperature and short time favour the kinetic product, high temperature and long time the thermodynamic one.
The phase rule counts freedom: more phases mean fewer variables you can change without one phase disappearing.
Water's phase diagram has a triple point where F = 0 and a critical point where the liquid-vapour boundary simply ends.
The Pb-Ag system freezes at a single eutectic temperature, and the reduced phase rule gives F′ = 0 there for fixed pressure.
bank_note: Long answers usually ask for a derivation or a labelled diagram plus a numerical part — the Gibbs equation, an integrated rate law, or the phase rule applied to water or the Pb-Ag eutectic.

bank.q: Define enthalpy, entropy and Gibbs free energy. Write the relation connecting them and state the condition for spontaneity at constant temperature and pressure.
outline: H = U + PV with each term named
ΔS = q_rev/T, units J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹
G = H − TS
ΔG < 0 spontaneous, ΔG = 0 equilibrium, ΔG > 0 non-spontaneous
Standard conditions stated

bank.q: A reaction has ΔH negative but does not occur at room temperature. Explain how the Gibbs equation accounts for this, and find the temperature above which it becomes spontaneous.
outline: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS applied
negative ΔH favours, negative ΔS opposes
term −TΔS becomes positive when ΔS is negative
set ΔG = 0, T = ΔH/ΔS
correct units K

bank.q: Distinguish order of reaction from molecularity. Give one example each of a reaction of order zero, one and two.
outline: order from experiment, may be zero, fractional or negative
molecularity from a single elementary step, whole number
zero order example: decomposition on a saturated catalyst surface
first order example: radioactive or SN1 hydrolysis
second order example: ester saponification

bank.q: Derive the integrated rate law for a first order reaction and define half-life. Show that the half-life is independent of initial concentration.
outline: rate = −d[A]/dt = k[A]
separation and integration to ln[A] = ln[A]₀ − kt
exponential form [A] = [A]₀e^(−kt)
graph of ln[A] against t is a straight line of slope −k

bank.q: State the Arrhenius equation. Explain the meaning of the activation energy and the pre-exponential factor, and how a plot of ln k against 1/T gives Ea.
outline: k = A e^(−Ea/RT), symbols named
Ea is the minimum energy for a productive collision
A relates to collision frequency and orientation
ln k = ln A − Ea/RT
slope = −Ea/R, intercept = ln A

bank.q: For a reaction ΔH = −92 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS = −198 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Calculate ΔG at 298 K and state whether the reaction is spontaneous. Find the temperature at which ΔG = 0.
outline: convert ΔS to kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ before adding
ΔG = −33 kJ mol⁻¹, so spontaneous at 298 K
T = ΔH/ΔS ≈ 465 K
significance of the crossover temperature stated

bank.q: A first order reaction is 40 percent complete in 25 minutes. Calculate the rate constant and the half-life, and the time needed for 90 percent completion.
outline: use 100/60 for 40 percent completion
t₉₀ = 2.303 log 10 / k ≈ 113 min

bank.q: Apply the phase rule to the water system. Find the degrees of freedom at the triple point, along the ice-water boundary and inside the single-phase regions. Explain each answer in words.
outline: F = C − P + 2 with C = 1
triple point P = 3 gives F = 0
melting curve P = 2 gives F = 1
single-phase region P = 1 gives F = 2
physical meaning of each value stated

bank.q: For the Pb-Ag system, state the reduced phase rule and calculate the degrees of freedom at the eutectic point, in the two-phase regions and in the melt. Sketch the diagram and label the eutectic temperature and composition.
outline: F′ = C − P + 1 for fixed pressure
C = 2, eutectic P = 3 gives F′ = 0
two-phase region P = 2 gives F′ = 1
melt P = 1 gives F′ = 2
eutectic labelled as the lowest freezing point, both solids separate together

bank.q: Compare kinetic and thermodynamic control of a reaction using an energy profile. Explain why the kinetic product forms at low temperature and the thermodynamic product at high temperature, and how the reaction time matters.
outline: two products drawn on one energy diagram
kinetic product: lower activation barrier, higher G
thermodynamic product: higher barrier, lower G
Boltzmann population of barriers at low temperature
reversibility and equilibration given enough time or heat
one organic or industrial example of each

bank.q: Draw and explain the phase diagram of water. Discuss the triple point, the critical point, the slopes of the three curves and the unusual negative slope of the ice-water line.
outline: axes labelled T and P, three regions and three curves
triple point at 273.16 K and 611.7 Pa, F = 0
critical point near 647 K and 22.06 MPa, boundary ends
positive slopes for sublimation and vapourisation curves, Clausius-Clapeyron
negative slope for fusion because ice is less dense than water
metastable supercooled water mentioned if space allows

bank.q: Derive the Gibbs phase rule from the number of intensive variables and the number of constraints. Then show how it reduces to F′ = C − P + 1 for condensed systems, and judge why the reduced form is used for alloys and salts.
outline: count of composition variables and phase-equilibrium constraints
F = C − P + 2 derived step by step
pressure fixed at 1 atm removes one variable
why metal and salt systems are studied at atmospheric pressure
limitation: the rule counts variables, it says nothing about amounts

bank.q: Free energy decides the direction of a chemical change; the same stability idea decides where phase boundaries lie. Explain both statements with the Gibbs equation, a rate comparison and the phase rule, using one example from each part.
outline: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS as the general stability test
ΔG = 0 marks equilibrium, which underlies a phase boundary
kinetic barrier decides speed, free energy decides direction, both needed
phase rule count of freedom, triple point F = 0
clapeyron slope and vapour pressure link G of two phases
one worked numerical or phase diagram example at the end

glossary.def: The study of energy changes, direction and extent of change, without reference to time.
Everything outside the system that can exchange energy or matter with it.
A property whose value depends only on the present state, not on the path taken, such as H, S and G.
The total energy stored inside a system, including kinetic and potential energy of its particles.
A change that releases heat to the surroundings, so ΔH is negative.
A change that absorbs heat from the surroundings, so ΔH is positive.
The entropy of an isolated system never decreases; spontaneous changes raise the total entropy.
Pure substance at 1 bar pressure, with solutions at 1 mol L⁻¹, usually at 298 K.
The extra energy a collision needs before products can form.
A substance that lowers the activation energy and speeds a reaction without being consumed.
A second order reaction run with one reactant in large excess, so its concentration looks constant and the order behaves as one.
The highest energy arrangement on the reaction path, at the top of the activation barrier.
A one-dimensional progress variable used to plot energy along the path from reactants to products.
A system with a single phase throughout, such as a salt solution.
A system with two or more phases, such as ice floating in water.
A system of solids and liquids only, where the pressure effect is small enough to ignore.
A curve on a phase diagram where two phases coexist in equilibrium.
Direct change from solid to vapour without passing through the liquid state.
The pressure of vapour in equilibrium with its liquid or solid at a given temperature.
Melting of a compound to a liquid of the same composition, so the compound survives as a phase.
A solid mixture of two or more metals, often with a eutectic or compound in its phase diagram.
A property that does not depend on the amount of material, such as temperature, pressure and mole fraction.
A property that depends on the amount of material, such as volume, mass and total energy.
A relation linking vapour pressure to temperature and the enthalpy of vapourisation.
